newsitem.title: INDIA: Global rally drives Indian aluminium stocks higher.
newsitem.headline: Global rally drives Indian aluminium stocks higher.

text.p: India's aluminium stocks have outstripped Bombay's benchmark index on a rally in global prices, but a sharp slowdown in local demand is likely to cushion the impact at home, analysts said on Wednesday.
"LME (London Metal Exchange) prices are firm and showing signs of going up further but prices in the domestic market have not yet responded," said an analyst at a European brokerage.
Analysts are underweight on most commodity-linked stocks except aluminium, where global prices have skyrocketed to around $1,600 a tonne from $1,300 in mid-October.
Share prices of leading aluminium makers Hindalco, NALCO and Indal have responded by jumping an average 30 percent since the start of November.
They have outperformed Bombay's benchmark stocks index, which rose less than 10 percent in the same period.
But industry sources said falling demand -- triggered by an overall industrial slowdown -- could put a dampener on the outlook for the sector.

"Industrial activity has slowed down in the last few months and unless activity gears up in sectors like construction, local prices will stay at current levels," said an official at NALCO, the country's largest aluminium maker.
"Besides, the earlier slump in prices had led to a good-size increase in imports," he said.
Small consumers imported large quantities of the metal in October, about the time aluminium hit a two-year low on the LME.
"Last year's interest-free credit periods and discounts offered by companies to consumers have also remained static," the analyst at the European brokerage said.
He said falling orders for rolled products from the transport sector and spending cuts in the electricity sector -- which uses wire rods -- had contributed to the lower demand.
"Then there are the production cutbacks in consumer durables where inventories have piled up," he said.
Analysts said an overcapacity in certain sectors was also responsible for keeping a cap on local prices.
"There's already a 20 percent overcapacity in the rolled products segment," said Chetan Ahya, analyst at Caspian Securities.
Primary metal makers -- like NALCO and Hindalco -- are likely to show an increase in exports in the second half of the financial year 1996/97 (April-March), analysts said.
The NALCO official said metal exports were likely to rise to 60,000 tonnes from 49,128 tonnes in 1995/96. NALCO produced 192,288 tonnes of metal last year.
"Our exports had already touched 36,000 tonnes by the end of December," he said.
"There may be some setback in turnover and profit margins but the year is not bad for the industry."
